paras: The abduction of Henry Burney was the removal of a Black prisoner from the Laurens County jail at Dublin, Georgia, by a party of masked men on the night of Tuesday, January 10, 1888. Burney was being held on a charge of knocking down and robbing J. M. Reinhart of Dublin. Georgia papers said only that he was believed, or possibly, lynched, while national news summaries reported flatly that he had been lynched, placing the event in Laurens County, Kentucky, or at Macon. A month later a Savannah paper reported that he had been sentenced to four years' imprisonment.

According to the Savannah Morning News, J. M. Reinhart was assaulted and robbed while returning home from his place of business on the night of Saturday, December 24, 1887. An earlier item in the same paper gave the night as Friday and the sum as $1,600, and said that Burney, described as "colored," was under arrest on the charge. The Atlanta Constitution's Dublin correspondent called Burney "a negro of desperate character," and the Morning News said he bore "a very unsavory reputation." The Morning News added, however, that many people had openly doubted his guilt and that sympathy had been aroused on his behalf.

In a Dublin special dated January 12, the Constitution reported that five men woke Jailer Arnan on Tuesday night and took the jail keys from him by force. The five then joined about twenty others waiting outside, and the whole party went to the jail and took Burney away. The Morning News described the group as a mob of twenty masked men who overpowered the jailer and obtained the keys from his residence. By the Constitution's account, nothing had been heard of the men or their prisoner since.

No report of a body, an inquest or any arrest of the masked men appears in the coverage. On February 11 the Morning News stated in a one-line item that Burney, "charged with robbing a saloon keeper named Reinhart of $2,000 at Dublin," had been sentenced to four years' imprisonment. The same item said that many of the best citizens of Laurens County did not believe he was guilty, but it did not explain how he had come back into custody.

The two Georgia papers that covered the seizure treated its outcome as uncertain. The Constitution headed its dispatch "An Outrage Upon Law in Laurens County" and wrote that Burney was "believed to have been lynched." The Morning News instead wrote that he had been "presumably, set at liberty" and that it was only "barely possible" he had been lynched, while calling the sympathy shown him "misguided."

Outside Georgia the story circulated as a single sentence in weekly news summaries printed between January 18 and 21 in papers in Minnesota, Iowa, Wisconsin, Dakota and Illinois. These items stated that Henry "Buney" had been taken from the jail in Laurens County, "Ky., on the 13th and lynched," adding only that he was accused of robbery. The River Falls Journal spelled the name Burney, and the Citizen in Illinois gave the day as Friday. A second summary item, printed in the Narragansett Herald on January 21 and later in North and South Carolina weeklies, placed the event at Macon, Ga., and said the masked men had "lynched him." Neither wire version repeated the doubts expressed in the Georgia reports.

Accounts differ on whether Burney was killed at all. The wire summaries reported a lynching as fact, the Constitution's correspondent said only that one was believed, and the Morning News thought it more likely that he had been set free. The Morning News's later report of his sentence, if accurate, would mean that he survived, although it is a single brief item.

The place and date also vary: the Dublin-datelined reports put the seizure in Laurens County, Georgia, on Tuesday night, while the summaries gave Kentucky or Macon and "the 13th," a date later than the local reports themselves.

bases: A masked party of about twenty to twenty-five men overpowered the jailer and took an accused Black prisoner from the Laurens County, Georgia, jail (A2, A3); wire summaries called it a lynching (A4, A13), though whether he was killed is disputed (A2, A16).

A masked group of twenty or more illegally took Burney from jail (A2, A3), but the local reports only believed or thought it 'barely possible' he was lynched, one suggested he was set free (A2), and a later item says he was sentenced to four years (A16); only distant wire briefs state a lynching as fact (A4, A13).

The seizure from jail is corroborated by two Georgia papers (A2, A3), but the killing reported in wire briefs (A4, A13) is doubted locally (A2, A3) and contradicted by a later report of his sentencing (A16).

The Dublin-datelined Constitution special and the Georgia column of the Morning News are the specific local sources; the Kentucky and Macon placements appear only in distant summary items.

The Constitution special is dated January 12 and the Morning News item ran January 13, both saying 'Tuesday night'; the wire's 'the 13th' is later than the local reports themselves. No opened brief says 'the 18th'.
